narrative:
The model estimated a 75.8% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt, which is why your law school application was rejected. This does not mean failure is certain; it means the model judged the risk high enough to deny admission at this time.

The denial was driven most strongly by your third-year class standing. You were in the second decile, well below the average accepted student, who was around the sixth decile. That was the single most influential factor and it pushed the prediction toward bar exam failure. Your first-year class standing was the second most important factor: you were in the third decile, also below the accepted average, and it likewise pushed toward failure. Your LSAT score was the third most important factor. At 29.30 it is below the accepted average of 37.18, but in this particular prediction it acted as a modest counterweight toward passing; it was simply not enough to offset the academic-standing signals.

Next, ask admissions whether you can appeal or provide context, such as extenuating circumstances. Speak with an advisor about strengthening your academic record, retaking the LSAT if permitted, and applying to programs that review applicants holistically. Treat the prediction as a warning to address, not a final judgment.
